Abstract:
Vision-language models (VLMs) pretrained on large-scale multimodal datasets encode rich visual and linguistic knowledge, making them a strong foundation for robotics. Rather than training robotic policies from scratch, recent approaches adapt VLMs into vision-language-action (VLA) models that enable natural language-driven perception and control. However, existing VLAs are typically massive--often with billions of parameters--leading to high training costs and limited real-world deployability. Moreover, they rely on academic and industrial datasets, overlooking the growing availability of community-collected data from affordable robotic platforms. In this work, we present SmolVLA, a small, efficient, and community-driven VLA that drastically reduces both training and inference costs, while retaining competitive performance. SmolVLA is designed to be trained on a single GPU and deployed on consumer-grade GPUs or even CPUs. To further improve responsiveness, we introduce an asynchronous inference stack decoupling perception and action prediction from action execution, allowing higher control rates with chunked action generation. Despite its compact size, SmolVLA achieves performance comparable to VLAs that are 10x larger. We evaluate SmolVLA on a range of both simulated as well as real-world robotic benchmarks and release all code, pretrained models, and training data.

The excerpt identifies two principal robot-arm architectures used in self-driving laboratories and related scientific automation: six-axis articulated arms (six degrees of freedom, or six-DOF) and SCARAs (Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arms). SCARAs use a central column, two rotational joints for movement in the XY plane, vertical Z-axis actuation, and a compliant end-effector joint. Their design supports rapid, precise, repeatable movements, but they are less suited to complex three-dimensional object manipulation. Six-DOF articulated arms provide largely unconstrained positioning and greater spatial flexibility, analogous to a human arm, although they generally trade some speed and kinematic simplicity for versatility. In SDLs, six-DOF arms often connect instruments into a coordinated automated workflow and can perform common laboratory manipulations such as transferring vials, adding reagents, and operating instruments that would otherwise require manual use. Abstract:
Numerous grasp planning algorithms have been proposed since the 1980s. The grasping literature has expanded rapidly in recent years, building on greatly improved vision systems and computing power. Methods have been proposed to plan stable grasps on known objects (exact 3D model is available), familiar objects (e.g. exploiting a-priori known grasps for different objects of the same category), or novel object shapes observed during task execution. Few of these methods have ever been compared in a systematic way, and objective performance evaluation of such complex systems remains problematic. Difficulties and confounding factors include different assumptions and amounts of a-priori knowledge in different algorithms; different robots, hands, vision systems and setups in different labs; and different choices or application needs for grasped objects. Also, grasp planning can use different grasp quality metrics (including empirical or theoretical stability measures) or other criteria, e.g., computational speed, or combination of grasps with reachability considerations. While acknowledging and discussing the outstanding difficulties surrounding this complex topic, we propose a methodology for reproducible experiments to compare the performance of a variety of grasp planning algorithms. Our protocol attempts to improve the objectivity with which different grasp planners are compared by minimizing the influence of key components in the grasping pipeline, e.g., vision and pose estimation. The protocol is demonstrated by evaluating two different grasp planners: a state-of-the-art model-free planner and a popular open-source model-based planner. We show results from real-robot experiments with a 7-DoF arm and 2-finger hand, as well as simulation-based evaluations.

Abstract:
Pick-and-place operations constitute the majority of today's industrial robotic applications. However, comparability and reproducibility of results has remained an issue that delays further advances in this field. Evaluation of manipulation systems can be carried out at different levels, but for the final application the performance of the overall system is the critical one. This paper proposes a benchmarking framework for pick-and-place systems, inspired by a typical task in the logistic domain: picking up fruits and vegetables from a container and placing them in an order bin. The framework uses an easy-to-reproduce environment, a publicly available object set, and guidelines for creating scenarios of different complexity. The proposed benchmark is applied to evaluate the performance of four variants of a robotic system with different end-effectors.

The use of benchmarks is a widespread and scientifically meaningful practice to validate performance of different approaches to the same task. In the context of robot grasping the use of common object sets has emerged in recent years, however no dominant protocols and metrics to test grasping pipelines have taken root yet. In this letter, we present version 1.0 of GRASPA, a benchmark to test effectiveness of grasping pipelines on physical robot setups. This approach tackles the complexity of such pipelines by proposing different metrics that account for the features and limits of the test platform. As an example application, we deploy GRASPA on the iCub humanoid robot and use it to benchmark our grasping pipeline. Abstract:
In this work, we describe a multi-object grasping benchmark to evaluate the grasping and manipulation capabilities of robotic systems in both pile and surface scenarios. The benchmark introduces threerobot multi-object grasping benchmarking protocols designed to challenge different aspects of robotic manipulation. These protocols are: 1) the Only-Pick-Once protocol, which assesses the robot's ability to efficiently pick multiple objects in a single attempt; 2) the Accurate pick-transferring protocol, which evaluates the robot's capacity to selectively grasp and transport a specific number of objects from a cluttered environment; and 3) the Pick-transferring-all protocol, which challenges the robot to clear an entire scene by sequentially grasping and transferring all available objects. These protocols are intended to be adopted by the broader robotics research community, providing a standardized method to assess and compare robotic systems' performance in multi-object grasping tasks. We establish baselines for these protocols using standard planning and perception algorithms on a Barrett hand, Robotiq parallel jar gripper, and the Pisa/IIT Softhand-2, which is a soft underactuated robotic hand. We discuss the results in relation to human performance in similar tasks as well.

The training dataset contains over 92,000 labeled random grasps, collected in parallel on two cells; approximately 23% succeed. For reaching, the task is to control the six joint velocities so the end-effector reaches a specified 3D target. The SO-101 Bench is a simulated, language-conditioned spatial-manipulation benchmark built using an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It evaluates four core task types—placing an object in a bin, placing one object next to another, placing an object between two reference objects, and moving an object in a specified direction—organized into five task families. Evaluation covers 138 objects divided into seen objects, unseen instances, and unseen classes, with 916 simulated episodes. Performance is reported as mean success across the 15 task-family-by-object-split cells, with additional subsets testing held-out visual appearances (ROBUST), rotate-to-fit planning (PLAN), and remembering occluded objects (MEM). Policies are fine-tuned on 3,629 simulated teleoperation demonstrations under equal compute budgets. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the strongest learned policies achieve about 61% mean success, while spatial placement, novel object classes, and rotate-to-fit planning remain difficult. An LLM agent that writes manipulation code and delegates grasping to a learned policy reaches 83.2%. The benchmark’s sim-to-real validation reports that five policies trained without real data preserve their exact ranking on the physical SO-101 in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman ρ = 1.00; MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates absolute success.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000050

From text 'collins2024rampabenchmark pages 3-4'.

Jack Collins, Mark Robson, Jun Yamada, Mohan Sridharan, Karol Janik, and Ingmar Posner. Ramp: a benchmark for evaluating robotic assembly manipulation and planning. IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, 9:9-16, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/lra.2023.3330611, doi:10.1109/lra.2023.3330611. This article has 35 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

RAMP (a benchmark for robotic assembly manipulation and planning) evaluates both planning and physical execution in open-ended, long-horizon robotic assembly tasks. It uses reconfigurable beams and pegs to create easy, medium, and hard assemblies, with goal configurations specified through an image and XML; the benchmark is intended to test generalisation to new designs as well as perception, state estimation, planning, control, execution, recovery, and learning. The excerpt specifies single-arm manipulation, but allows any robot with a manipulator arm, sensors for state estimation, and a choice of gripper. {"answer": "# Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories and the Low-Cost Manipulation Frontier: A Literature Review with Repeatable Benchmarks

## 1. Field Overview: Robot Arms in Automated and Self-Driving Laboratories

### 1.1 Defining the Field

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate robotic automation with artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific discovery. The most comprehensive review is Tom et al. (2024), which provides "an in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in SDL technology, its applications across various scientific disciplines, and the potential implications for research and industry" (pqac-00000001). That review distinguishes three hardware tiers for SDL automation: special-purpose systems costing approximately $1 million, general-purpose robotic-arm systems at roughly $10,000, and open hardware at $100–$2,000 (pqac-00000001). The two principal arm architectures used in SDLs are six-axis articulated arms (6-DOF) and SCARA arms; six-DOF arms provide "largely unconstrained positioning and greater spatial flexibility, analogous to a human arm" and are used to "connect instruments into a coordinated automated workflow" (pqac-00000000).

Moran et al. (2026, peer-reviewed in *npj Robotics*) provide a more recent survey focused specifically on robotics in SDLs, identifying six-DOF arms and SCARAs as the two dominant architectures, and noting that robotic subsystems may be commercial, bespoke, or open-source (pqac-00000000). The ADePT framework (Salazar-Villacis & Benyahia, 2026, peer-reviewed in *Communications Chemistry*) introduced four core dimensions—Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity—for systematically evaluating autonomous laboratory robotics, moving the field beyond simple task-completion metrics toward a holistic assessment of capability proficiency (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061).

### 1.2 Landmark Systems

**Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2)** defined the field with the first mobile robotic chemist, using a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm (14 kg payload, 0.1 mm repeatability) mounted on a KMR mobile base. The system achieved positioning accuracy of "±0.12 mm" translation and "±0.005°" orientation after a touch-sensitive six-point calibration method, and "ran 43 batches of 16 samples, totaling 688 experiments" autonomously over eight days (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023).

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7)** demonstrated autonomous mobile robots for exploratory synthetic chemistry, integrating mobile robots with LC-MS and benchtop NMR, showing that "a synthesis laboratory can be integrated into an autonomous laboratory by using mobile robots that operate equipment and make decisions in a human-like way" (pqac-00000001).

**UR5e-based systems** have been widely adopted: a six-DOF UR5e (0.03 mm repeatability, 850 mm reach) was used for modular flow-reactor assembly for retrosynthetic planning (pqac-00000005), for chemical experiment automation with demonstration-based programming (pqac-00000024), and as the manipulation platform in mobile SDL configurations (pqac-00000026). The AutoBio simulation benchmark also uses UR5e with Robotiq 2F-85 parallel gripper for biology laboratory tasks (pqac-00000009).

**Franka Emika Panda** (7-DOF, ~0.1 mm repeatability, 3 kg payload) serves as the standard manipulation research platform in FurnitureBench and RAMP (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000053).

The "frugal twin" concept proposed by Lo et al. (2024, peer-reviewed in *Digital Discovery*; DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00223c) explicitly advocates low-cost surrogates of high-cost experimental platforms, establishing the philosophical foundation for democratizing SDL hardware (pqac-00000001).

### 1.3 The Low-Cost and Open-Source Movement

The movement toward low-cost manipulation hardware accelerated from 2019 onward with several key contributions:

- **REPLAB (Yang et al., 2019, ICRA; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390)**: A ~$2,000 standardized work cell (70×40×60 cm) built around a Trossen WidowX arm, RGB-D camera, and defined workspace, providing a "task definition, evaluation protocol, performance measures, and a dataset of over 50,000 grasp attempts" (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). **Peer-reviewed.**

- **Blue (Gealy et al., 2019, ICRA; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794236)**: A 7-DOF quasi-direct-drive arm with "prototype bill-of-materials cost of $3,328" and an estimated consumer price near $5,000, providing ~4 mm repeatability and 2 kg burst payload at full extension (pqac-00000012). **Peer-reviewed.**

- **ALOHA (Zhao et al., 2023; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2304.13705)**: A bimanual leader-follower teleoperation system costing ~$20,000 (later described as "roughly $4,900 for an ALOHA arm"), paired with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) for end-to-end imitation learning (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000034). **Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed as a journal article).**

- **LeRobot (Cadène et al., 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.22818)**: An open-source library for end-to-end robot learning, explicitly supporting "low-cost, open-source robots like SO-10X and ALOHA" that "cost a fraction of proprietary industrial arms." The SO-100 and SO-101 are among the most adopted platforms, with 319,586 downloads and 58,299 episodes for SO-101 on the Hugging Face hub (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036). **Preprint.**

- **Open Robot Hardware (Patel et al., 2023, *IEEE RA Magazine*; DOI: 10.1109/MRA.2022.3225725)**: A comprehensive review of 80+ open-hardware projects noting that open hardware "lowers the barrier of entry to new technologies and can further accelerate innovation in robotics." **Peer-reviewed.**

## 2. Comparison of Arms Across Cost Tiers

The following table summarizes robot arms from industrial SDL platforms through to ultra-low-cost open-source arms, identifying which specifications are peer-reviewed versus nominal or unvalidated.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Critical gap for the user's setup:** No peer-reviewed journal article or major conference paper was found that independently validates the AgileX PiPER's repeatability, payload, or manipulation performance. Its specifications should therefore be treated as manufacturer claims until independently verified. The SO-100 and SO-101 similarly lack peer-reviewed metrological characterization, though their manipulation performance has been benchmarked in preprints via task success rates.

## 3. Published Benchmarks Reproducible on Low-Cost Arms

The following table details published benchmarks with sufficient protocol specificity that they can be adapted or directly reproduced on PiPER and SO-101 platforms.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 3.1 Protocols Most Directly Relevant to the User's Setup

**ALOHA ACT (preprint).** The original ALOHA study used 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task (except 100 for Thread Velcro) and evaluated each task over 25 physical trials with one training seed. The six real-world tasks—Slide Ziploc, Slot Battery, Open Cup, Thread Velcro, Prep Tape, and Put On Shoe—yielded final-task success rates of 88%, 96%, 84%, 20%, 64%, and 92%, respectively (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017). Success was judged by binary task completion with intermediate milestones scored as well. This protocol can be adapted to a single PiPER arm (substituting single-arm tasks) or to SO-101 leader-follower pairs.

**Mobile ALOHA (preprint).** Fu et al. extended ALOHA with a mobile base and co-training on static ALOHA data, reporting that "co-training can increase success rates by up to 90%" on mobile manipulation tasks. Whole-task co-trained success rates ranged from 40% (Cook Shrimp, 20 demonstrations) to 95% (Wipe Wine, 50 demonstrations) (pqac-00000013).

**SO-101 demonstration-scaling study (Cowling, 2026; preprint).** This study is the most directly comparable benchmark for SO-101 arms. A single pick-and-place task (pick green ball, ignore two red distractors, place in basket) was evaluated with nested demonstration budgets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200. ACT was evaluated over 40 episodes per budget on ten fixed placements with a 30-second limit. ACT success scaled from "1/40 (3%) at 12 demonstrations to 37/40 (93%) at 100 demonstrations" (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). SmolVLA peaked at "21/40 (53%) at 50 demonstrations" then declined; Diffusion Policy performed poorly without trimming idle demonstration lead-in frames (pqac-00000043). **This protocol is immediately repeatable on SO-101 hardware with the LeRobot stack.**

**SO-101 Bench (Hickok, 2026; preprint).** A simulated, language-conditioned spatial-manipulation benchmark using an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101, with 916 evaluation episodes across four task families (Bin, Next-to, Between, Move). Success must "persist for 5 seconds" and tasks impose geometric constraints (e.g., "the target must move at least 1 inch, remain untouched at the end, and non-target objects must not move more than 1 inch") (pqac-00000031). The best learned policies achieved approximately 61% mean success, while "five policies trained without real data preserve their exact ranking on the physical SO-101" (Spearman ρ = 1.00), though "simulation overestimated absolute success by 9–31 percentage points" (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029).

**REPLAB grasping (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2019).** A test set of 20 toys is grasped with a cumulative-success-rate metric; "the protocol terminates after success or after 10 unsuccessful attempts, followed by sweeping the arm over the workspace floor to perturb objects" (pqac-00000008). The dataset of labeled grasps (23% baseline success) provides ground truth for training grasping policies. This benchmark's $2,000 cell design is comparable to the PiPER system cost.

**RAMP (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L 2024).** Uses "AprilTags attached to beams and pegs" with "wrist-mounted and bird's-eye cameras" for state estimation (pqac-00000051). Each assembly is attempted five consecutive times, and "a successful insertion requires the peg to enter the correct hole with no stem visible, sit flush with the joint surface, and pin the required two joints" (pqac-00000050). This benchmark is directly relevant to setups using AprilTags and wrist cameras.

**FurnitureBench (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2025).** Uses a Franka Panda with "three Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D cameras, including wrist/front views" and measures assembly-phase completion across eight 3D-printable furniture pieces. A reproducibility study showed that "10 participants independently built new environments" and a trained policy "achieved an average of 84% of the original performance" (pqac-00000040). While designed for Franka, the 3D-printable furniture pieces and phase-completion metrics could be adapted to any 6-DOF arm with parallel gripper.

### 3.2 Protocols Using Industrial Arms (for Comparison Baselines)

**Burger et al. mobile robotic chemist (peer-reviewed, *Nature* 2020).** The KUKA LBR iiwa completed 688 chemistry experiments with calibrated positioning accuracy of ±0.12 mm, tested with 100 calibration trials (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). This establishes an upper bound for laboratory manipulation precision.

**AutoBio biology laboratory benchmark (preprint, 2025).** Nine biology-laboratory tasks using UR5e and ALOHA arms, including pipetting, centrifuge-tube manipulation, and thermal-cycler operation. Scoring is generally binary: "success requires satisfying pose and contact requirements at checkpoints and terminal states; exceeding the time limit is failure" (pqac-00000009).

## 4. The Imitation Learning Pipeline: From ALOHA to LeRobot

The imitation learning approach used in the user's setup has a clear lineage:

### 1.1 Defining the Field

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate robotic automation with artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific discovery. The most comprehensive review is Tom et al. (2024), which provides "an in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in SDL technology, its applications across various scientific disciplines, and the potential implications for research and industry" (pqac-00000001). Moran et al. (2026, peer-reviewed in *npj Robotics*) provide a more recent survey focused specifically on robotics in SDLs, identifying six-DOF arms and SCARAs as the two dominant architectures, and noting that robotic subsystems may be commercial, bespoke, or open-source (pqac-00000000). The ADePT framework (Salazar-Villacis & Benyahia, 2026, peer-reviewed in *Communications Chemistry*) introduced four core dimensions—Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity—for systematically evaluating autonomous laboratory robotics, moving the field beyond simple task-completion metrics toward a holistic assessment of capability proficiency (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061).

**Burger et al. **Dai et al. **UR5e-based systems** have been widely adopted: a six-DOF UR5e (0.03 mm repeatability, 850 mm reach) was used for modular flow-reactor assembly for retrosynthetic planning (pqac-00000005), for chemical experiment automation with demonstration-based programming (pqac-00000024), and as the manipulation platform in mobile SDL configurations (pqac-00000026). The "frugal twin" concept proposed by Lo et al. (2024, peer-reviewed in *Digital Discovery*; DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00223c) explicitly advocates low-cost surrogates of high-cost experimental platforms, establishing the philosophical foundation for democratizing SDL hardware (pqac-00000001).

The system achieved positioning accuracy of "±0.12 mm" translation and "±0.005°" orientation after a touch-sensitive six-point calibration method, and "ran 43 batches of 16 samples, totaling 688 experiments" autonomously over eight days (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 4-6, burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56, burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3).

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7)** demonstrated autonomous mobile robots for exploratory synthetic chemistry, integrating mobile robots with LC-MS and benchtop NMR, showing that "a synthesis laboratory can be integrated into an autonomous laboratory by using mobile robots that operate equipment and make decisions in a human-like way" (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 5-6).

**UR5e-based systems** have been widely adopted: a six-DOF UR5e (0.03 mm repeatability, 850 mm reach) was used for modular flow-reactor assembly for retrosynthetic planning (salazarvillacis2026theadeptframework pages 3-4), for chemical experiment automation with demonstration-based programming (sasaki2025roboticsystemfor pages 6-8), and as the manipulation platform in mobile SDL configurations (sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 6-9). The AutoBio simulation benchmark also uses UR5e with Robotiq 2F-85 parallel gripper for biology laboratory tasks (lan2025autobioasimulation pages 13-16).

**Franka Emika Panda** (7-DOF, ~0.1 mm repeatability, 3 kg payload) serves as the standard manipulation research platform in FurnitureBench and RAMP (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 3-4, collins2024rampabenchmark pages 1-2).

The "frugal twin" concept proposed by Lo et al. (2024, peer-reviewed in *Digital Discovery*; DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00223c) explicitly advocates low-cost surrogates of high-cost experimental platforms, establishing the philosophical foundation for democratizing SDL hardware (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 5-6).

### 1.3 The Low-Cost and Open-Source Movement

The movement toward low-cost manipulation hardware accelerated from 2019 onward with several key contributions:

- **REPLAB (Yang et al., 2019, ICRA; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390)**: A ~$2,000 standardized work cell (70×40×60 cm) built around a Trossen WidowX arm, RGB-D camera, and defined workspace, providing a "task definition, evaluation protocol, performance measures, and a dataset of over 50,000 grasp attempts" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 1-2, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 1-2). **Peer-reviewed.**

- **Blue (Gealy et al., 2019, ICRA; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794236)**: A 7-DOF quasi-direct-drive arm with "prototype bill-of-materials cost of $3,328" and an estimated consumer price near $5,000, providing ~4 mm repeatability and 2 kg burst payload at full extension (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 6-8). **Peer-reviewed.**

- **ALOHA (Zhao et al., 2023; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2304.13705)**: A bimanual leader-follower teleoperation system costing ~$20,000 (later described as "roughly $4,900 for an ALOHA arm"), paired with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) for end-to-end imitation learning (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8, hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2). **Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed as a journal article).**

- **LeRobot (Cadène et al., 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.22818)**: An open-source library for end-to-end robot learning, explicitly supporting "low-cost, open-source robots like SO-10X and ALOHA" that "cost a fraction of proprietary industrial arms." The SO-100 and SO-101 are among the most adopted platforms, with 319,586 downloads and 58,299 episodes for SO-101 on the Hugging Face hub (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2, cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 13-16). **Preprint.**

- **Open Robot Hardware (Patel et al., 2023, *IEEE RA Magazine*; DOI: 10.1109/MRA.2022.3225725)**: A comprehensive review of 80+ open-hardware projects noting that open hardware "lowers the barrier of entry to new technologies and can further accelerate innovation in robotics." **Peer-reviewed.**

### 3.1 Protocols Most Directly Relevant to the User's Setup

**ALOHA ACT (preprint).** The original ALOHA study used 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task (except 100 for Thread Velcro) and evaluated each task over 25 physical trials with one training seed. The six real-world tasks—Slide Ziploc, Slot Battery, Open Cup, Thread Velcro, Prep Tape, and Put On Shoe—yielded final-task success rates of 88%, 96%, 84%, 20%, 64%, and 92%, respectively (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 8-10). Success was judged by binary task completion with intermediate milestones scored as well. This protocol can be adapted to a single PiPER arm (substituting single-arm tasks) or to SO-101 leader-follower pairs.

**Mobile ALOHA (preprint).** Fu et al. extended ALOHA with a mobile base and co-training on static ALOHA data, reporting that "co-training can increase success rates by up to 90%" on mobile manipulation tasks. Whole-task co-trained success rates ranged from 40% (Cook Shrimp, 20 demonstrations) to 95% (Wipe Wine, 50 demonstrations) (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 5-7).

**SO-101 demonstration-scaling study (Cowling, 2026; preprint).** This study is the most directly comparable benchmark for SO-101 arms. A single pick-and-place task (pick green ball, ignore two red distractors, place in basket) was evaluated with nested demonstration budgets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200. ACT was evaluated over 40 episodes per budget on ten fixed placements with a 30-second limit. ACT success scaled from "1/40 (3%) at 12 demonstrations to 37/40 (93%) at 100 demonstrations" (cowling2026from12to pages 9-12, cowling2026from12to pages 3-5). SmolVLA peaked at "21/40 (53%) at 50 demonstrations" then declined; Diffusion Policy performed poorly without trimming idle demonstration lead-in frames (cowling2026from12to pages 9-12). **This protocol is immediately repeatable on SO-101 hardware with the LeRobot stack.**

**SO-101 Bench (Hickok, 2026; preprint).** A simulated, language-conditioned spatial-manipulation benchmark using an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101, with 916 evaluation episodes across four task families (Bin, Next-to, Between, Move). Success must "persist for 5 seconds" and tasks impose geometric constraints (e.g., "the target must move at least 1 inch, remain untouched at the end, and non-target objects must not move more than 1 inch") (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 6-8). The best learned policies achieved approximately 61% mean success, while "five policies trained without real data preserve their exact ranking on the physical SO-101" (Spearman ρ = 1.00), though "simulation overestimated absolute success by 9–31 percentage points" (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2, hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 2-4).

**REPLAB grasping (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2019).** A test set of 20 toys is grasped with a cumulative-success-rate metric; "the protocol terminates after success or after 10 unsuccessful attempts, followed by sweeping the arm over the workspace floor to perturb objects" (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 4-5). The dataset of labeled grasps (23% baseline success) provides ground truth for training grasping policies. This benchmark's $2,000 cell design is comparable to the PiPER system cost.

**RAMP (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L 2024).** Uses "AprilTags attached to beams and pegs" with "wrist-mounted and bird's-eye cameras" for state estimation (collins2024rampabenchmark pages 5-7). Each assembly is attempted five consecutive times, and "a successful insertion requires the peg to enter the correct hole with no stem visible, sit flush with the joint surface, and pin the required two joints" (collins2024rampabenchmark pages 3-4). This benchmark is directly relevant to setups using AprilTags and wrist cameras.

**FurnitureBench (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2025).** Uses a Franka Panda with "three Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D cameras, including wrist/front views" and measures assembly-phase completion across eight 3D-printable furniture pieces. A reproducibility study showed that "10 participants independently built new environments" and a trained policy "achieved an average of 84% of the original performance" (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 3-4). While designed for Franka, the 3D-printable furniture pieces and phase-completion metrics could be adapted to any 6-DOF arm with parallel gripper.

### 3.2 Protocols Using Industrial Arms (for Comparison Baselines)

**Burger et al. mobile robotic chemist (peer-reviewed, *Nature* 2020).** The KUKA LBR iiwa completed 688 chemistry experiments with calibrated positioning accuracy of ±0.12 mm, tested with 100 calibration trials (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 4-6, burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). This establishes an upper bound for laboratory manipulation precision.

**AutoBio biology laboratory benchmark (preprint, 2025).** Nine biology-laboratory tasks using UR5e and ALOHA arms, including pipetting, centrifuge-tube manipulation, and thermal-cycler operation. Scoring is generally binary: "success requires satisfying pose and contact requirements at checkpoints and terminal states; exceeding the time limit is failure" (lan2025autobioasimulation pages 13-16).

## 4. The Imitation Learning Pipeline: From ALOHA to LeRobot

The imitation learning approach used in the user's setup has a clear lineage:

1. **ACT (Zhao et al., 2023; preprint)** introduced "Action Chunking with Transformers," a generative model over action sequences that "allows the robot to learn 6 difficult tasks in the real world, such as opening a translucent condiment cup and slotting a battery with 80-90% success, with only 10 minutes worth of demonstrations" (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8).

2. **Mobile ALOHA (Fu et al., 2024; preprint)** demonstrated that "co-training with existing static ALOHA datasets boosts performance on mobile manipulation tasks" with "50 demonstrations for each task" (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 5-7).

3. **LeRobot (Cadène et al., 2026; preprint)** unified the software stack, providing teleoperation-to-deployment pipelines for SO-100/101 arms. The SO-100/101 became the most popular community platform with over 78,000 episodes contributed to the hub (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 13-16).

4. **Cowling (2026; preprint)** provided the first controlled scaling study on SO-101, showing that ACT trained from scratch overtook pretrained VLA policies at approximately 100 demonstrations, achieving 93% success on a pick-and-place task (cowling2026from12to pages 9-12).

5. **SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025; preprint)** demonstrated a small, efficient VLA model that "achieves performance comparable to VLAs that are 10x larger," evaluated on SO-100 (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2).

## 5. Where No Published Evidence Exists

The following gaps were identified in the peer-reviewed literature:

- **AgileX PiPER**: No peer-reviewed paper was found reporting independent verification of PiPER's repeatability, payload, workspace, or manipulation benchmarks. The arm's specifications remain manufacturer claims.

- **SO-101 metrological characterization**: No published work provides a calibrated repeatability value (e.g., ISO 9283 pose repeatability) for the SO-100 or SO-101. Task success rates from preprints exist, but no positional accuracy assessment using a measurement instrument (e.g., laser tracker, CMM) has been published.

- **Low-cost arms in chemistry/biology SDL workflows**: No published system was found that uses SO-100/101 or PiPER-class arms for actual chemistry or biology experimentation in a self-driving laboratory. All published SDLs use industrial arms (KUKA, UR, ABB) or specialized liquid handlers. The "frugal twin" concept exists in review form (Lo et al., 2024) but has not been demonstrated with sub-$2,000 general-purpose arms for scientific experimentation.

- **Head-to-head comparisons**: No published paper directly compares PiPER, SO-101, or similar low-cost arms against UR5e or Franka on identical laboratory tasks with a controlled protocol.

- **AprilTag-based calibration for laboratory precision**: While RAMP uses AprilTags for assembly localization (collins2024rampabenchmark pages 5-7) and Cooper's LIRA module uses "fiducial markers attached to each station" (brass2026amobilerobotic pages 7-10), no published study quantifies how AprilTag-based calibration affects manipulation accuracy on low-cost servo-based arms specifically.

## 6. Recommended Tests for Your Setup

Based on the literature review, the following tests can be repeated on PiPER (6-DOF, ~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower (~$200) arms:

**Tier 1 — Immediately repeatable with existing protocols:**
1. **Cowling pick-and-place scaling test** on SO-101: collect 12–200 demonstrations of a ball-to-basket task, train ACT via LeRobot, evaluate 40 episodes per budget on 10 fixed placements with 30 s timeout. Compare against published ACT curve (3%→93%) (cowling2026from12to pages 9-12).
2. **REPLAB-style grasping**: construct a work cell, define 20 test objects, measure cumulative success rate over grasp attempts with stop-after-10-failures protocol (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 4-5).

**Tier 2 — Adaptable with minor modifications:**
3. **ALOHA ACT tasks** (single-arm variants): adapt Slide Ziploc, Slot Battery, or Open Cup tasks to PiPER; collect 50 demonstrations and evaluate 25 trials per task (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8).
4. **RAMP assembly** with AprilTags: 3D-print beam and peg components, attach AprilTags, use wrist and fixed cameras for localization, run 5 consecutive assembly attempts (collins2024rampabenchmark pages 3-4, collins2024rampabenchmark pages 5-7).

**Tier 3 — Novel contributions (filling literature gaps):**
5. **ISO 9283-style positional repeatability test**: command the arm to a set of predefined poses across the workspace, measure achieved position with a calibrated measurement tool, report RP (pose repeatability). No such test has been published for PiPER or SO-101.
6. **Laboratory vial-transfer benchmark**: measure grasp-and-place success rate for standard laboratory vials (e.g., 10 mL GC vials), comparing against Burger et al.'s ±0.12 mm calibrated positioning (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 4-6).

## 7. Summary

The field of robot arms in self-driving laboratories has evolved from expensive, proprietary industrial systems (KUKA, UR5e, ~$35k–$100k+) toward increasingly affordable platforms. The "low-cost, open-source" movement, catalyzed by ALOHA (2023) and LeRobot (2026), has produced platforms costing $120–$200 (SO-101) to ~$2,000 (PiPER, REPLAB). However, the literature reveals a critical maturity gap: industrial arms used in SDLs have peer-reviewed metrological characterization and demonstrated scientific workflows, whereas ultra-low-cost arms have only preprint-level task-success benchmarks and no demonstrated SDL applications. Filling this gap—by running repeatable benchmarks on low-cost arms and comparing directly against published industrial-arm baselines—represents a clear opportunity for new contributions to the field.

# Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories and the Low-Cost Manipulation Frontier: A Literature Review with Repeatable Benchmarks

## 1. Field Overview: Robot Arms in Automated and Self-Driving Laboratories

### 1.1 Defining the Field

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate robotic automation with artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific discovery. The most comprehensive review is Tom et al. (2024), which provides "an in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in SDL technology, its applications across various scientific disciplines, and the potential implications for research and industry" (pqac-00000001). That review distinguishes three hardware tiers for SDL automation: special-purpose systems costing approximately $1 million, general-purpose robotic-arm systems at roughly $10,000, and open hardware at $100–$2,000 (pqac-00000001). The two principal arm architectures used in SDLs are six-axis articulated arms (6-DOF) and SCARA arms; six-DOF arms provide "largely unconstrained positioning and greater spatial flexibility, analogous to a human arm" and are used to "connect instruments into a coordinated automated workflow" (pqac-00000000).

Moran et al. (2026, peer-reviewed in *npj Robotics*) provide a more recent survey focused specifically on robotics in SDLs, identifying six-DOF arms and SCARAs as the two dominant architectures, and noting that robotic subsystems may be commercial, bespoke, or open-source (pqac-00000000). The ADePT framework (Salazar-Villacis & Benyahia, 2026, peer-reviewed in *Communications Chemistry*) introduced four core dimensions—Adaptability and Learning, Dexterity, Perception, and Task Complexity—for systematically evaluating autonomous laboratory robotics, moving the field beyond simple task-completion metrics toward a holistic assessment of capability proficiency (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061).

### 1.2 Landmark Systems

**Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2)** defined the field with the first mobile robotic chemist, using a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm (14 kg payload, 0.1 mm repeatability) mounted on a KMR mobile base. The system achieved positioning accuracy of "±0.12 mm" translation and "±0.005°" orientation after a touch-sensitive six-point calibration method, and "ran 43 batches of 16 samples, totaling 688 experiments" autonomously over eight days (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023).

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7)** demonstrated autonomous mobile robots for exploratory synthetic chemistry, integrating mobile robots with LC-MS and benchtop NMR, showing that "a synthesis laboratory can be integrated into an autonomous laboratory by using mobile robots that operate equipment and make decisions in a human-like way" (pqac-00000001).

**UR5e-based systems** have been widely adopted: a six-DOF UR5e (0.03 mm repeatability, 850 mm reach) was used for modular flow-reactor assembly for retrosynthetic planning (pqac-00000005), for chemical experiment automation with demonstration-based programming (pqac-00000024), and as the manipulation platform in mobile SDL configurations (pqac-00000026). The AutoBio simulation benchmark also uses UR5e with Robotiq 2F-85 parallel gripper for biology laboratory tasks (pqac-00000009).

**Franka Emika Panda** (7-DOF, ~0.1 mm repeatability, 3 kg payload) serves as the standard manipulation research platform in FurnitureBench and RAMP (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000053).

The "frugal twin" concept proposed by Lo et al. (2024, peer-reviewed in *Digital Discovery*; DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00223c) explicitly advocates low-cost surrogates of high-cost experimental platforms, establishing the philosophical foundation for democratizing SDL hardware (pqac-00000001).

### 1.3 The Low-Cost and Open-Source Movement

The movement toward low-cost manipulation hardware accelerated from 2019 onward with several key contributions:

- **REPLAB (Yang et al., 2019, ICRA; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390)**: A ~$2,000 standardized work cell (70×40×60 cm) built around a Trossen WidowX arm, RGB-D camera, and defined workspace, providing a "task definition, evaluation protocol, performance measures, and a dataset of over 50,000 grasp attempts" (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). **Peer-reviewed.**

- **Blue (Gealy et al., 2019, ICRA; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794236)**: A 7-DOF quasi-direct-drive arm with "prototype bill-of-materials cost of $3,328" and an estimated consumer price near $5,000, providing ~4 mm repeatability and 2 kg burst payload at full extension (pqac-00000012). **Peer-reviewed.**

- **ALOHA (Zhao et al., 2023; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2304.13705)**: A bimanual leader-follower teleoperation system costing ~$20,000 (later described as "roughly $4,900 for an ALOHA arm"), paired with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) for end-to-end imitation learning (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000034). **Preprint (not yet peer-reviewed as a journal article).**

- **LeRobot (Cadène et al., 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.22818)**: An open-source library for end-to-end robot learning, explicitly supporting "low-cost, open-source robots like SO-10X and ALOHA" that "cost a fraction of proprietary industrial arms." The SO-100 and SO-101 are among the most adopted platforms, with 319,586 downloads and 58,299 episodes for SO-101 on the Hugging Face hub (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036). **Preprint.**

- **Open Robot Hardware (Patel et al., 2023, *IEEE RA Magazine*; DOI: 10.1109/MRA.2022.3225725)**: A comprehensive review of 80+ open-hardware projects noting that open hardware "lowers the barrier of entry to new technologies and can further accelerate innovation in robotics." **Peer-reviewed.**

### 3.1 Protocols Most Directly Relevant to the User's Setup

**ALOHA ACT (preprint).** The original ALOHA study used 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task (except 100 for Thread Velcro) and evaluated each task over 25 physical trials with one training seed. The six real-world tasks—Slide Ziploc, Slot Battery, Open Cup, Thread Velcro, Prep Tape, and Put On Shoe—yielded final-task success rates of 88%, 96%, 84%, 20%, 64%, and 92%, respectively (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017). Success was judged by binary task completion with intermediate milestones scored as well. This protocol can be adapted to a single PiPER arm (substituting single-arm tasks) or to SO-101 leader-follower pairs.

**Mobile ALOHA (preprint).** Fu et al. extended ALOHA with a mobile base and co-training on static ALOHA data, reporting that "co-training can increase success rates by up to 90%" on mobile manipulation tasks. Whole-task co-trained success rates ranged from 40% (Cook Shrimp, 20 demonstrations) to 95% (Wipe Wine, 50 demonstrations) (pqac-00000013).

**SO-101 demonstration-scaling study (Cowling, 2026; preprint).** This study is the most directly comparable benchmark for SO-101 arms. A single pick-and-place task (pick green ball, ignore two red distractors, place in basket) was evaluated with nested demonstration budgets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200. ACT was evaluated over 40 episodes per budget on ten fixed placements with a 30-second limit. ACT success scaled from "1/40 (3%) at 12 demonstrations to 37/40 (93%) at 100 demonstrations" (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). SmolVLA peaked at "21/40 (53%) at 50 demonstrations" then declined; Diffusion Policy performed poorly without trimming idle demonstration lead-in frames (pqac-00000043). **This protocol is immediately repeatable on SO-101 hardware with the LeRobot stack.**

**SO-101 Bench (Hickok, 2026; preprint).** A simulated, language-conditioned spatial-manipulation benchmark using an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101, with 916 evaluation episodes across four task families (Bin, Next-to, Between, Move). Success must "persist for 5 seconds" and tasks impose geometric constraints (e.g., "the target must move at least 1 inch, remain untouched at the end, and non-target objects must not move more than 1 inch") (pqac-00000031). The best learned policies achieved approximately 61% mean success, while "five policies trained without real data preserve their exact ranking on the physical SO-101" (Spearman ρ = 1.00), though "simulation overestimated absolute success by 9–31 percentage points" (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029).

**REPLAB grasping (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2019).** A test set of 20 toys is grasped with a cumulative-success-rate metric; "the protocol terminates after success or after 10 unsuccessful attempts, followed by sweeping the arm over the workspace floor to perturb objects" (pqac-00000008). The dataset of labeled grasps (23% baseline success) provides ground truth for training grasping policies. This benchmark's $2,000 cell design is comparable to the PiPER system cost.

**RAMP (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L 2024).** Uses "AprilTags attached to beams and pegs" with "wrist-mounted and bird's-eye cameras" for state estimation (pqac-00000051). Each assembly is attempted five consecutive times, and "a successful insertion requires the peg to enter the correct hole with no stem visible, sit flush with the joint surface, and pin the required two joints" (pqac-00000050). This benchmark is directly relevant to setups using AprilTags and wrist cameras.

**FurnitureBench (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2025).** Uses a Franka Panda with "three Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D cameras, including wrist/front views" and measures assembly-phase completion across eight 3D-printable furniture pieces. A reproducibility study showed that "10 participants independently built new environments" and a trained policy "achieved an average of 84% of the original performance" (pqac-00000040). While designed for Franka, the 3D-printable furniture pieces and phase-completion metrics could be adapted to any 6-DOF arm with parallel gripper.

### 3.2 Protocols Using Industrial Arms (for Comparison Baselines)

**Burger et al. mobile robotic chemist (peer-reviewed, *Nature* 2020).** The KUKA LBR iiwa completed 688 chemistry experiments with calibrated positioning accuracy of ±0.12 mm, tested with 100 calibration trials (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). This establishes an upper bound for laboratory manipulation precision.

**AutoBio biology laboratory benchmark (preprint, 2025).** Nine biology-laboratory tasks using UR5e and ALOHA arms, including pipetting, centrifuge-tube manipulation, and thermal-cycler operation. Scoring is generally binary: "success requires satisfying pose and contact requirements at checkpoints and terminal states; exceeding the time limit is failure" (pqac-00000009).

## 4. The Imitation Learning Pipeline: From ALOHA to LeRobot

The imitation learning approach used in the user's setup has a clear lineage:

1. **ACT (Zhao et al., 2023; preprint)** introduced "Action Chunking with Transformers," a generative model over action sequences that "allows the robot to learn 6 difficult tasks in the real world, such as opening a translucent condiment cup and slotting a battery with 80-90% success, with only 10 minutes worth of demonstrations" (pqac-00000015).

2. **Mobile ALOHA (Fu et al., 2024; preprint)** demonstrated that "co-training with existing static ALOHA datasets boosts performance on mobile manipulation tasks" with "50 demonstrations for each task" (pqac-00000013).

3. **LeRobot (Cadène et al., 2026; preprint)** unified the software stack, providing teleoperation-to-deployment pipelines for SO-100/101 arms. The SO-100/101 became the most popular community platform with over 78,000 episodes contributed to the hub (pqac-00000036).

4. **Cowling (2026; preprint)** provided the first controlled scaling study on SO-101, showing that ACT trained from scratch overtook pretrained VLA policies at approximately 100 demonstrations, achieving 93% success on a pick-and-place task (pqac-00000043).

5. **SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025; preprint)** demonstrated a small, efficient VLA model that "achieves performance comparable to VLAs that are 10x larger," evaluated on SO-100 (pqac-00000034).

## 5. Where No Published Evidence Exists

The following gaps were identified in the peer-reviewed literature:

- **AgileX PiPER**: No peer-reviewed paper was found reporting independent verification of PiPER's repeatability, payload, workspace, or manipulation benchmarks. The arm's specifications remain manufacturer claims.

- **SO-101 metrological characterization**: No published work provides a calibrated repeatability value (e.g., ISO 9283 pose repeatability) for the SO-100 or SO-101. Task success rates from preprints exist, but no positional accuracy assessment using a measurement instrument (e.g., laser tracker, CMM) has been published.

- **Low-cost arms in chemistry/biology SDL workflows**: No published system was found that uses SO-100/101 or PiPER-class arms for actual chemistry or biology experimentation in a self-driving laboratory. All published SDLs use industrial arms (KUKA, UR, ABB) or specialized liquid handlers. The "frugal twin" concept exists in review form (Lo et al., 2024) but has not been demonstrated with sub-$2,000 general-purpose arms for scientific experimentation.

- **Head-to-head comparisons**: No published paper directly compares PiPER, SO-101, or similar low-cost arms against UR5e or Franka on identical laboratory tasks with a controlled protocol.

- **AprilTag-based calibration for laboratory precision**: While RAMP uses AprilTags for assembly localization (pqac-00000051) and Cooper's LIRA module uses "fiducial markers attached to each station" (pqac-00000025), no published study quantifies how AprilTag-based calibration affects manipulation accuracy on low-cost servo-based arms specifically.

## 6. Recommended Tests for Your Setup

Based on the literature review, the following tests can be repeated on PiPER (6-DOF, ~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower (~$200) arms:

**Tier 1 — Immediately repeatable with existing protocols:**
1. **Cowling pick-and-place scaling test** on SO-101: collect 12–200 demonstrations of a ball-to-basket task, train ACT via LeRobot, evaluate 40 episodes per budget on 10 fixed placements with 30 s timeout. Compare against published ACT curve (3%→93%) (pqac-00000043).
2. **REPLAB-style grasping**: construct a work cell, define 20 test objects, measure cumulative success rate over grasp attempts with stop-after-10-failures protocol (pqac-00000008).

**Tier 2 — Adaptable with minor modifications:**
3. **ALOHA ACT tasks** (single-arm variants): adapt Slide Ziploc, Slot Battery, or Open Cup tasks to PiPER; collect 50 demonstrations and evaluate 25 trials per task (pqac-00000015).
4. **RAMP assembly** with AprilTags: 3D-print beam and peg components, attach AprilTags, use wrist and fixed cameras for localization, run 5 consecutive assembly attempts (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

**Tier 3 — Novel contributions (filling literature gaps):**
5. **ISO 9283-style positional repeatability test**: command the arm to a set of predefined poses across the workspace, measure achieved position with a calibrated measurement tool, report RP (pose repeatability). No such test has been published for PiPER or SO-101.
6. **Laboratory vial-transfer benchmark**: measure grasp-and-place success rate for standard laboratory vials (e.g., 10 mL GC vials), comparing against Burger et al.'s ±0.12 mm calibrated positioning (pqac-00000020).

## 7. Summary

The field of robot arms in self-driving laboratories has evolved from expensive, proprietary industrial systems (KUKA, UR5e, ~$35k–$100k+) toward increasingly affordable platforms. The "low-cost, open-source" movement, catalyzed by ALOHA (2023) and LeRobot (2026), has produced platforms costing $120–$200 (SO-101) to ~$2,000 (PiPER, REPLAB). However, the literature reveals a critical maturity gap: industrial arms used in SDLs have peer-reviewed metrological characterization and demonstrated scientific workflows, whereas ultra-low-cost arms have only preprint-level task-success benchmarks and no demonstrated SDL applications. Filling this gap—by running repeatable benchmarks on low-cost arms and comparing directly against published industrial-arm baselines—represents a clear opportunity for new contributions to the field.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies two principal robot-arm architectures used in self-driving laboratories and related scientific automation: six-axis articulated arms (six degrees of freedom, or six-DOF) and SCARAs (Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arms). SCARAs use a central column, two rotational joints for movement in the XY plane, vertical Z-axis actuation, and a compliant end-effector joint. Their design supports rapid, precise, repeatable movements, but they are less suited to complex three-dimensional object manipulation. Six-DOF articulated arms provide largely unconstrained positioning and greater spatial flexibility, analogous to a human arm, although they generally trade some speed and kinematic simplicity for versatility. In SDLs, six-DOF arms often connect instruments into a coordinated automated workflow and can perform common laboratory manipulations such as transferring vials, adding reagents, and operating instruments that would otherwise require manual use. The excerpt does not provide purchase prices, operating costs, payloads, reach, speed ratings, or specific commercial models. It also notes that robotic subsystems may be commercial turnkey systems or bespoke/custom-built platforms, potentially incorporating additive manufacturing and open-source software. Thus, the provided material supports architecture, qualitative specifications, and tasks, but not cost comparisons or detailed manufacturer-level specifications.

contexts.context: The excerpt distinguishes specialized, general-purpose, and open-hardware robotic systems used in self-driving laboratories. Specialized platforms include gantry systems with positive-displacement pipettes, such as SPT LabTech Mosquito and OpenTrons OT, which dispense microliter quantities and enable high-throughput parallel experiments in multi-well plates. Flexible automation may instead use robotic arms: the mobile robotic chemist of Burger et al. moved around a conventional laboratory, operated multiple instruments, searched photocatalyst mixtures, and was reconfigured for solubility screening and crystallization. General-purpose arms can physically interact with tools and objects, reducing dependence on proprietary equipment, but perception and decision-making remain challenges; they are also less efficient and harder to parallelize than specialized systems. Other demonstrated arm-based tasks include crystal retrieval by scraping vial walls, powder grinding, liquid pouring with visual or weight feedback, molecule synthesis using a robot-operated syringe pump, operating electronic or manual pipettes, solid dispensing, and electrode polishing. Open-hardware examples include Sidekick, with a 3D-printed chassis and home-built syringe pumps, although it handles only limited liquid identities. The table gives approximate hardware costs: special-purpose systems about $1 million, general-purpose systems about $10,000, and open hardware $100–2,000, excluding associated software or construction costs.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes REPLAB benchmarking, but contains no information about ALOHA or other specific low-cost robot-arm benchmarks. REPLAB’s grasping benchmark uses a test set of 20 toys, selected to include feasible stable grasps; objects are varied in shape and size, with approximately half hard plastic and half soft toys. A grasp attempt is generated from a segmented point-cloud object: a cluster is selected, grasp coordinates are sampled around its center, and the angle is randomized or chosen using baseline-specific rules. Testing reports cumulative success rate (CSR), defined as the number of successfully grasped objects versus the number of attempts. The protocol terminates after success or after 10 unsuccessful attempts, followed by sweeping the arm over the workspace floor to perturb objects. The training dataset contains over 92,000 labeled random grasps, collected in parallel on two cells; approximately 23% succeed. For reaching, the task is to control the six joint velocities so the end-effector reaches a specified 3D target. Joint angles and end-effector position are observations, and performance is measured by distance to the target over training time; the per-step reward is negative Euclidean distance. The excerpt does not state the total number of reaching trials or a reaching success-rate percentage.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports two difficult ALOHA ACT imitation-learning tasks. For candy unwrapping, the policy was trained with 50 demonstrations. In an initial 10-trial evaluation, it picked up the candy in 10/10 trials, pulled both ends in 8/10, but successfully opened the wrapper in 0/10. Because the seam was difficult to perceive, a second protocol used 10 trials for each of 5 candies; the policy successfully unwrapped 3/5 candies (60%). For opening a small ziploc bag lying flat, ACT was also trained with 50 demonstrations. It consistently learned the initial pickup, but struggled with the three subsequent mid-air manipulation steps: adjusting the bag for the other gripper, grasping the pulling region, and pulling it open; no aggregate final success rate is provided in this excerpt. The excerpt also describes cable-tie insertion and unstacking-cup tasks used in a user study. Cable-tie insertion required picking up one end, grasping the other mid-air, and coordinating both hands to insert the tie into its hole. Unstacking cups required grasping the upper cup and shaking it apart or using the other gripper. Six participants performed three consecutive attempts per setting after two minutes of adaptation.

The reported demonstration counts were: Wipe Wine (50), Cook Shrimp (20), Rinse Pan (50), Use Cabinet (50), Call Elevator (50), Push Chairs (50), and High Five (20). contexts.context: The excerpt reports ACT imitation-learning evaluation on nine underwater bimanual tasks, with one separately trained policy per task. Each task was evaluated in 10 trials, giving 90 baseline ACT trials overall. The first seven tasks used 10 demonstrations each: block hand-over (pass and receive a block), hand-over then place (transfer, receive, and place), block stacking (align and stack two blocks), sequential transfer (complete successive route legs), bimanual lifting (grasp and lift jointly), cooperative insertion (hold a cup and insert a block), and lid opening (hold a container and remove its lid). The final two buoyancy-driven sponge tasks used 50 demonstrations each: surface hand-over (grasp and transfer a floating sponge) and release and catch (release and intercept a rising sponge). Reported ACT success rates were: block hand-over 10/10; hand-over then place 6/10; block stacking 9/10; sequential transfer 10/10; bimanual lifting 10/10; cooperative insertion 9/10; lid opening 7/10; surface hand-over 4/10; and release and catch 3/10. The baseline used a 100-step execution horizon.

contexts.context: The ALOHA ACT experiments evaluated six real-world and two simulated bimanual manipulation tasks. The simulated tasks were Cube Transfer and Bimanual Insertion; the real tasks were Slide Ziploc, Slot Battery, Open Cup, Thread Velcro, Prep Tape, and Put On Shoe. Real-task demonstrations were collected through ALOHA teleoperation: 50 demonstrations per task, except Thread Velcro, which used 100, for approximately 350 real demonstrations total. The simulated experiments recorded 50 successful scripted demonstrations and 50 successful human demonstrations for each task. Real-world results used one training seed and 25 evaluations per task. ACT’s real-task success rates were: Slide Ziploc—92% Grasp, 96% Pinch, 88% Open; Slot Battery—100% Grasp, 100% Place, 96% Insert; Open Cup—100% Tip Over, 96% Grasp, 84% Open Lid; Thread Velcro—92% Lift, 40% Grasp, 20% Insert; Prep Tape—96% Grasp, 92% Cut, 72% Handover, 64% Hang; Put On Shoe—100% Lift, 92% Insert, 92% Support, 92% Secure. Simulated results are reported separately for scripted versus human training: Cube Transfer achieved 97|82, 90|60, and 86|50% across its subtasks; Bimanual Insertion achieved 93|76, 90|66, and 32|20%.

contexts.context: Burger et al. used a KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR) arm mounted on a KUKA Mobile Platform (KMP) mobile base. The arm had a maximum payload of 14 kg and an 820 mm reach; the combined robot and base weighed approximately 430 kg, and its movement was restricted to 0.5 m s−1 for safety. The mobile platform’s uncalibrated navigation repeatability/precision was better than ±10 mm in x-y position and less than ±2.5° in orientation. Because this was insufficient for delicate tasks such as vial placement, the researchers applied a touch-sensitive six-point calibration method. This improved positioning accuracy to ±0.12 mm and orientation accuracy to ±0.005°, broadly comparable to a human operator for delicate manipulations. During the autonomous search, the system ran 43 batches of 16 samples, totaling 688 experiments. Eleven results were discarded due to workflow errors or excessive oxygen caused by faulty vial seals, leaving 677 retained experimental results.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes SO-101 Bench as a language-conditioned tabletop-manipulation benchmark using a single SO-101 arm. It evaluates four tasks, scored as five families: placing every object in a moving plastic bin (separately with one object and four objects), placing one object next to another, placing one object between two referents, and moving an object in a commanded direction until it reaches a boundary formed by another object. The tasks test object identification among distractors, grasping unfamiliar geometries, transport, precise placement, relational and spatial reasoning, and robustness to partial occlusion. The bin task requires identifying, grasping, transporting, and depositing objects; the next-to task requires close placement without disturbing other objects; the between task requires centered placement sensitive to object extent, orientation, and fine positioning; and the directional task requires pushing or carrying along a straight path. The benchmark uses seen, unseen-instance/seen-class, and unseen-class object splits, with some unseen classes held private to prevent leakage. contexts.context: The SO-101 Bench evaluates spatial manipulation by a SO-101 arm in a scanned-room digital twin and on a real robot, using household objects divided into seen, unseen-object/seen-class, and unseen-class splits. The reported task families are binning objects, placing a target next to a referent, placing it between two referents, and moving it toward or up to a boundary object; the evaluation includes one- and four-object bin variants. Success is state-based and must persist for 5 seconds. Bin success requires every object to be inside the bin footprint and untouched; next-to and between use geometric distance/collinearity constraints; move requires forward progress or contact with the object ahead, a path within 2 inches of straight, and minimal boundary-object displacement. The target must move at least 1 inch, remain untouched at the end, and non-target objects must not move more than 1 inch. The primary evaluation has 916 scored episodes across 15 task-family/split cells, with 30-second timeouts (75 seconds for four-object bins). Training used 3,629 simulated teleoperation episodes; approximately 4,400 real-robot teleoperation episodes were also released. contexts.context: The SO-101 Bench is a simulated, language-conditioned spatial-manipulation benchmark built using an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It evaluates four core task types—placing an object in a bin, placing one object next to another, placing an object between two reference objects, and moving an object in a specified direction—organized into five task families. Evaluation covers 138 objects divided into seen objects, unseen instances, and unseen classes, with 916 simulated episodes. Performance is reported as mean success across the 15 task-family-by-object-split cells, with additional subsets testing held-out visual appearances (ROBUST), rotate-to-fit planning (PLAN), and remembering occluded objects (MEM). Policies are fine-tuned on 3,629 simulated teleoperation demonstrations under equal compute budgets. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the strongest learned policies achieve about 61% mean success, while spatial placement, novel object classes, and rotate-to-fit planning remain difficult. An LLM agent that writes manipulation code and delegates grasping to a learned policy reaches 83.2%. The benchmark’s sim-to-real validation reports that five policies trained without real data preserve their exact ranking on the physical SO-101 in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman ρ = 1.00; MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates absolute success.

contexts.context: The SO-101 Bench paper describes a simulated, language-conditioned spatial-manipulation benchmark built around a single low-cost SO-101 arm and an Isaac Lab digital twin of the physical setup. It evaluates 138 household objects across seen objects, unseen objects from seen classes, and unseen classes, with additional ROBUST, PLAN, and MEM subsets. The four automatically scored task families are: placing every object in a bin; placing one object next to another; placing it between two objects; and moving it in a specified direction until reaching a boundary object. Tasks require identifying named objects among same-class distractors, grasping unfamiliar shapes, and satisfying spatial constraints; success is determined from simulator state, using feasibility-checked episodes. The primary evaluation contains 916 episodes across 15 task-family-by-split cells. The released datasets include 3,629 simulated teleoperated episodes and approximately 4,400 real episodes. In sim-to-real testing, five policies had identical rankings in simulation and on the real arm (Spearman ρ=1.00), though simulation overestimated success by 9–31 percentage points. On the broader leaderboard, the best learned policies scored around 61, while none exceeded 17% on PLAN. GPT-6.1 Sol achieved 83.2 overall and solved 75% of PLAN; with a learned-policy handoff it reached 85% on 60 paired episodes, versus 53% for Galaxea 0.5 alone.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes SO-101 Bench as a spatial-manipulation benchmark used to test whether a digital twin reproduces the difficulty and failure structure of the physical SO-101 arm, and whether simulation predicts real-world policy performance. The reported task families include spatial instructions such as “next to,” “between,” and “move,” evaluated across object-count bins (including 1-object and 4-object bins) and seen, unseen-object/seen-class, and unseen-class splits. Performance is reported as episode success: the real-only policy succeeds when the instructed manipulation is completed on the physical arm, while failures are classified as semantic (wrong object or referent), grasping (grasp, lift, or release failure), or placement (incorrect or imprecise placement). The main comparison contains 906 matched episodes across 15 task-by-split conditions. The real-only policy achieves 61% success (552/906), versus 45% (409/906) for the independently trained sim-only policy. Difficulty rankings correspond strongly across domains (Pearson r=0.86; Spearman ρ=0.74), while paired episode outcomes agree 66% of the time. LeRobot supports the arm throughout the pipeline, from teleoperation to deployment, and SO-100/101 platforms account for a large share of community datasets on Hugging Face. The text also notes that models such as SmolVLA and MolmoAct2 are trained or post-trained on community SO-100/101 data, but are generally starting points requiring task-specific fine-tuning; no released policy is reported to solve spatially constrained, language-conditioned SO-101 tasks out of the box in new environments with new objects.

The cited SO-101 benchmarks are physical-hardware evaluations involving tasks such as insertion, pouring, wiping, spatial grounding, relational placement, referential descriptions, ordinal position, and counting. The introduced SO-101 Bench instead provides simulation with four task types—Bin, Next to, Between, and Move—organized into five task families and evaluated on seen objects, unseen instances, and unseen classes. It reports 916 evaluation episodes and 3,629 simulated demonstrations. The best learned policies score around 61%, while an LLM agent combined with a learned grasping policy reaches 83.2%.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies FurnitureBench as a reproducible real-world benchmark for long-horizon furniture assembly. It includes eight 3D-printable furniture models—lamp, square table, drawer, cabinet, round table, desk, stool, and chair—and provides a standardized robot/environment setup, systematic task initialization, control software, and FurnitureSim. The benchmark evaluates both individual skills and complete assembly. Single-skill evaluation covers diverse subtasks such as grasping, inserting, and screwing, with the stated purpose of identifying challenges in insertion and screwing. The full-assembly benchmark measures performance over furniture assemblies containing up to 12 subtasks; the excerpt reports that imitation-learning and offline-reinforcement-learning methods achieve up to 2 of 12 subtasks on average. The system is designed around one robotic arm, and furniture pieces were modified so they could be assembled one-handed. The excerpt does not specify the number of evaluation trials, formal success criteria, or the make/model of the robot arm. It does mention more than 5,000 demonstrations and over 200 hours of collected data, but these are training/demo resources rather than an explicitly stated trial count.

contexts.context: Cowling reports a controlled comparison of ACT, Diffusion Policy, and SmolVLA on one physical pick-and-place task involving distractor objects, using a low-cost SO-101 arm. The study trained each policy on nested demonstration sets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 teleoperated demonstrations, with one fixed training recipe per policy. In total, the researchers collected 225 demonstrations and evaluated trained models on ten fixed object placements under a 30-second limit, scoring 1,340 episodes in 126 blocks. ACT was trained from scratch and showed the clearest improvement with more data: it achieved 1 success in 40 episodes with 12 demonstrations and 37/40 with 100 demonstrations. The excerpt does not give exact success counts for ACT at every demonstration size, nor exact counts for Diffusion Policy and SmolVLA. It reports that both Diffusion Policy and SmolVLA peaked near 50% success. Their results were substantially affected by initiation failures: SmolVLA never started moving in 47% of episodes, while Diffusion Policy rarely started until idle lead-in segments were removed from the training demonstrations. The authors stress that these are recipe- and task-specific results from one arm, not universal architectural rankings.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports scaling results for policies performing a ball-manipulation task on a low-cost arm: episodes were assessed by whether the arm started, reached the ball, carried it, and delivered it, with success requiring completion. ACT scaled most strongly with demonstrations, rising from 1/40 successes (3%) at 12 demonstrations, to 11/40 (28%) at 25, 18/40 (45%) at 50, 37/40 (93%) at 100, and 35/40 (88%) at 200. Its odds of success increased 3.89-fold per doubling of data. SmolVLA rose from 2/40 (5%) at 12 and 4/40 (10%) at 25 to 21/40 (53%) at 50, then fell to 14/40 (35%) at 100 and 15/40 (38%) at 200; the paper attributes much of this decline to episodes in which the arm never started. Diffusion Policy with trimmed demonstrations achieved 0/20 (0%), 6/20 (30%), 25/50 (50%), 6/30 (20%), and 12/30 (40%) at 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations, respectively. Untrimmed demonstrations performed poorly: 3/110 successes overall. The study emphasizes that ACT eventually overtook the pretrained alternative at higher data budgets, while SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked at 50 demonstrations.

contexts.context: RAMP (a benchmark for robotic assembly manipulation and planning) evaluates both planning and physical execution in open-ended, long-horizon robotic assembly tasks. It uses reconfigurable beams and pegs to create easy, medium, and hard assemblies, with goal configurations specified through an image and XML; the benchmark is intended to test generalisation to new designs as well as perception, state estimation, planning, control, execution, recovery, and learning. The excerpt specifies single-arm manipulation, but allows any robot with a manipulator arm, sensors for state estimation, and a choice of gripper. For reproducibility, an entire assembly class should be completed with unchanged code, and each assembly should be attempted five consecutive times; only the goal changes between runs. AprilTags are not described as a current required component. Rather, integrating April Tags for marker-based state estimation is listed as a possible future extension of the simulation environment. Performance prioritises accurate completion and short execution time. A successful insertion requires the peg to enter the correct hole with no stem visible, sit flush with the joint surface, and pin the required two joints; otherwise the completion percentage does not increase. Results include the time for each successful insertion, including plan-generation time.

A robot assembles beams into specified goal configurations, using pegs as fasteners.
